title: SaaS Validation Before You Build
audience: Independent developers who can build the SaaS and know that technical confidence is exactly what makes it easy to waste weeks or months on an idea nobody will pay for.
shortDescription: Make being wrong cheap. Test the customer, problem, urgency, and willingness to act before a plausible idea turns into two months of code and a launch nobody asked for.
coreOutcome: Leave with enough behavioral evidence to make a deliberate build, change, or stop decision before heavy development consumes the time and momentum.
problem: Building feels productive and familiar, so a technical founder can spend weeks proving the software can exist while the risk that matters most remains untouched: whether anyone cares enough to act.
hook: Do not spend two months proving the software can exist before proving anyone cares.
reframe:
For a developer, coding is seductive because progress is visible. The database works. The auth flow is done. The dashboard looks real. Customer research is messier. People contradict each other, cancel calls, say something sounds useful, and refuse to tell you what that praise is actually worth.

That asymmetry makes building feel safer even when it is the more expensive gamble. A month of development can answer “can this exist?” while leaving “will anyone change behavior or pay?” almost completely unanswered. Friendly comments and feature suggestions make the risk worse because they feel like validation without costing the prospect anything.

SaaS Validation Before You Build turns the idea into assumptions that can lose. You identify the customer, problem, urgency, current alternatives, and willingness to act, then choose evidence that would strengthen or weaken the case before you see the result. Conversations, access, introductions, pilots, and payment can all carry different weight. The goal is not certainty. It is making a bad idea cheap enough to abandon before your sunk cost starts arguing with you.

delivery.length: Implementation guide for assumption mapping, customer research, problem evidence, commitment tests, and build decisions.
delivery.worksheets: Riskiest-assumption map, interview guide, evidence log, commitment-test design, decision thresholds, and build-change-stop review.
delivery.time: Run the validation process before committing to heavy product development or a large MVP scope.

proof.title: “I would use that” and “I will do this now” are not the same evidence.
proof.body: The system records compliments separately from behavior that costs the prospect something, such as giving access to a workflow, joining a pilot, introducing a decision-maker, investing time, or paying. That makes enthusiasm harder to confuse with demand.
proof.before: Several people said the idea sounds useful, so start building the MVP.
proof.after: Define the risky assumption, choose the evidence that would support or weaken it, run the test, record behavior, and make the build decision against a threshold set in advance.

situation: The idea feels plausible and buildable, but the customer, problem, urgency, alternatives, and willingness to act remain largely assumptions.
commonFailure: Feature planning and friendly feedback create the feeling of momentum without reducing the commercial risk that nobody changes behavior or pays.
methodology: State falsifiable assumptions, identify the riskiest ones, collect problem evidence, test commitment with appropriate asks, record behavior, and compare the results with explicit build, revise, or stop criteria.
capabilities: Find the assumption most likely to make months of building commercially irrelevant
Collect customer behavior that carries more weight than compliments
Decide to build, change, or stop before sunk cost starts making the decision for you
contents: Audience definition and reachable early-customer selection
Problem interviews that separate evidence from encouragement
Current alternatives, switching friction, urgency, and problem cost
Commitment tests using time, access, introductions, pilots, or payment where appropriate
Build, revise, or stop thresholds set before the result is known
Validation review and handoff into MVP scope
whoItsFor: Indie and bootstrapped SaaS builders before heavy development
Developers with a plausible idea and very little behavioral evidence from potential customers
Technical founders who know their ability to build quickly can become a reason to validate too slowly
whoItsNotFor: Anyone seeking certainty or guaranteed product-market fit
Products that already have strong customer evidence and have earned the build decision
Anyone unwilling to talk to real potential customers or test commitment

faqs.question: Do I need a prototype first?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Many of the assumptions most likely to kill the business concern the customer and problem, and those can often be tested before a working product exists.

faqs.question: How many interviews prove the idea?
faqs.answer: No fixed interview count proves demand. The system looks at evidence quality, repeated patterns, contradictory evidence, and commitment rather than giving you a magic number that feels safe.

faqs.question: Does validation guarantee the SaaS will work?
faqs.answer: No. It makes one category of expensive mistake less likely. Product, pricing, acquisition, retention, and execution still have to work afterward.

faqs.question: What happens if the evidence is weak?
faqs.answer: You revise the audience, problem, or proposed approach, run a better test, or stop. A cheap no is a good outcome when the alternative is months of building.
